### [Workweek restrictions during the Great Depression](papers/labor-replication.qmd)

<div class="meta"><span>Labor Economics</span><span>Pierre Cahuc</span><span>M2</span><span class="grade">Grade: 18/20</span></div>

I replicate Fishback et al.’s study of the 1933 President’s Reemployment Agreement, examining workweek limits, employment, and earnings. Additional tests vary macroeconomic controls, clustering, estimation windows, and industry composition across the paper’s regression, bunching, and difference-in-differences designs. Most core results withstand these checks, while conflicting pre-trends qualify the weekly-earnings and payroll findings. An establishment-level earnings proxy provides a further check and produces effects of different magnitudes.

[Overview & paper →](papers/labor-replication.qmd)
:::

### [Food deserts and nutritional inequality](papers/urban-summary.qmd)

<div class="meta"><span>Urban Economics</span><span>Pierre-Philippe Combes</span><span>M2 · May 2026</span><span class="grade">Grade: 16/20</span></div>

This essay reviews Allcott et al. (2019), “Food Deserts and the Causes of Nutritional Inequality.” It explains the supermarket-entry and household-mover designs, the structural model of grocery demand, and the decomposition of nutritional inequality into supply and demand components. I discuss how the paper arrives at its conclusion that differences in demand explain most of the observed nutrition gap, and how that conclusion informs the comparison between retail-access policies and healthy-food subsidies.

[Overview & paper →](papers/urban-summary.qmd)
:::

### [Beyond access: modelling food demand](papers/urban-proposal.qmd)

<div class="meta"><span>Urban Economics</span><span>Pierre-Philippe Combes</span><span>M2 · May 2026</span><span class="grade">Grade: 18/20</span></div>

Building on Allcott et al. (2019), this proposal examines restrictions imposed by a static, partial-equilibrium model of grocery demand. I discuss retailer and spatial responses, habit formation, and the distinction between preferences and price sensitivity. The proposed extension allows implicit-price sensitivity to differ between product groups with higher and lower nutritional scores, using interactions with chain-level pricing instruments to study how that heterogeneity could affect the interpretation of nutritional inequality and subsidy simulations.

[Overview & paper →](papers/urban-proposal.qmd)
:::

### [“Labor Market Power, Self-Employment, and Development”](papers/development-referee.qmd)

[Paper by F. Amodio, P. Medina and M. Morlacco]{.paper-by}

<div class="meta"><span>Development Economics</span><span>Clément Imbert</span><span>M2 · April 2026</span><span class="grade">Grade: 18/20</span></div>

The paper by Amodio, Medina and Morlacco studies self-employment as an outside option in concentrated Peruvian labour markets. In my report, I question their identification of wage markdowns, since the electrification shock they use may also raise wages through rent-sharing, and I show that their model overstates how much earnings fall with employer concentration. I then propose an extension using the expansion of the Cajas Municipales microfinance network to test whether better self-employment opportunities raise wages more in concentrated labour markets.

[Overview & paper →](papers/development-referee.qmd)
:::

### [“Officer-Involved: The Media Language of Police Killings”](papers/law-referee.qmd)

[Paper by J. Moreno-Medina, A. Ouss, P. Bayer and B. A. Ba (NBER Working Paper, 2022)]{.paper-by}

<div class="meta"><span>Topics in Political, Public and Organizational Economics · Law &amp; Economics block</span><span>Roberto Galbiati</span><span>M2</span></div>

The paper by Moreno-Medina, Ouss, Bayer and Ba measures obfuscatory language in US news reports on police killings and relates it to support for the police. In my report, I argue that their evidence shows a correlation between police and media language rather than police reports driving media coverage, and I suggest an analysis of evidential markers such as “police say” to test it. I also question the donation outcome used in their experiment, propose the CES panel to account for respondents’ media exposure, and point to other differences across media outlets worth examining.

[Overview & paper →](papers/law-referee.qmd)
:::

### [“Does Tax-Benefit Linkage Matter for the Incidence of Payroll Taxes?”](papers/public-referee.qmd)

[Paper by A. Bozio et al. (2025)]{.paper-by}

<div class="meta"><span>Topics in Political, Public and Organizational Economics · Public Economics block</span><span>Antoine Ferey</span><span>M2</span></div>

The paper by Bozio et al. argues, using six French reforms, that the perceived link between a payroll tax and the benefits it funds determines how much of the tax is passed on to workers’ earnings. In my report, I argue that one of their no-linkage reforms is a tax cut, which employers may pass on less for reasons unrelated to linkage, and I propose the 2007 exemption of overtime hours as a test. I also suggest allowing perceived linkage to vary across workers, for instance by age, and controlling for industry-specific shocks.

[Overview & paper →](papers/public-referee.qmd)
:::
